style: calm, natural hesitations, like explaining to a friend
slides: So, when you finish a practice essay, you don't just put it away. You review it, fix it, and rewrite it.
Why? Well, while we're learning, just like in the quantitative sections, we don't practise under time pressure at first. We look at questions from every angle.
Same thing with the essay. I want to write as well as I can. Yes, the exam gives you thirty-five minutes, and in simulations I'll stick to thirty-five. But right now, I want to learn.
One of the best ways to get better is to review your own essay. Because when I review myself, I have to think.
If someone just writes down my mistakes for me, I only look at them. And I might make them again, or similar ones.
But when I have to find my own mistakes, I go much deeper. What parts does the paragraph have? Are the connectors in place? Is the thread clear? Is there repetition? Is my language high enough?

And you'll say: wow, I could have done that myself. And if you have a teacher or a friend who can read it, show it to them after your own review. Then their comments will teach you the things you really couldn't find yourself.
First, we review the timing.
We don't just take thirty-five minutes and stop. We use a stopwatch, and at every stage, we write down how long it took.
How long did planning take? The analysis, finding arguments, the skeleton. The opening? Argument one? Argument two? The rebuttal? The closing?
Then I compare. If the opening took me five or six minutes, I have a problem. And that's actually great, because now I know what to make shorter next time.
Now the essay itself. First, a general pass. There's no time pressure now. This isn't proofreading, it's a review.
I read the last sentence of the opening, that's my position, and then the first sentence of each paragraph. The key sentences.
In the rebuttal paragraph, I read both the counterargument and my weakening, which is in the middle of the paragraph.
The background doesn't matter right now, it's fixed content. So I check: is there a clear thread? Do the reasons actually support my position? Does this essay make sense?
Now we go deep. Every paragraph.
We read it, and check the flow of ideas inside the paragraph, its focus, and its cohesion.
And we ask: did this paragraph reach its goal? Remember, in each lesson, every paragraph had a goal for the essay, and a goal for the rater.
The opening was supposed to make a great first impression in language. So, did it or didn't it?
We also fix language mistakes, and lift the language where we can.
Not by stuffing in over-the-top expressions. There are plenty of words that aren't very high, but they still upgrade the essay.
Like: 'a lot of' becomes 'considerable'. 'Show' becomes 'demonstrate'. 'So' becomes 'therefore'. 'I mean' becomes 'that is'.
But only use it when it means exactly what you want. A difficult word used the wrong way costs you more than a simple one.
I fix everything I find, and I rewrite the essay. And comparing the two versions shows me how far I've come.
Now, a few more recommendations.
First, don't review it on the same day. Even after you write it, don't review it right away.
Why wait at least a night? Because right now, I'm biased toward the essay I just wrote. An hour or two later, I'm still inside it. I'm less critical.
Come back after a day, maybe two, and you look at it with a more critical eye. Your mistakes are much easier to see.
A great way to get better is to read official sample essays.
The official English samples come with three labels: strong, adequate, and weak.
And just a reminder. The essay is the part students tend to put the least work into, even though it's a quarter of the Verbal score.
Here's a tip. Read the sample first, decide what level it is and why, point to a specific part, and only then look at the label.
With strong essays, I try to understand why they're strong. The argument is really well supported. The language is so precise.
If you want to go deep, take a paragraph apart. Here's the key sentence, here's the development, here's an example, a comparison, a weakening of this type or that type.
And strong samples aren't all the same. Some will make you say: wow, amazing. And others... okay, I could write something like that too.
With adequate essays, I read, and I try to find the problems. Why is this one only adequate?
The development isn't good enough here. A step in the explanation is missing. The same point comes back in other words. The language isn't right here.
I try to find the problems, and also how they could be fixed.
And the weak samples? There, the benefit is mainly to feel good about yourself.
It sometimes makes me laugh, but it can really help. You reviewed an essay, found loads of mistakes, and you feel like you can't write and you're not getting better?
Read a few weak essays, and you'll say: I'm not as bad as I thought.
And one more tip. Something I really, really recommend.
You finished an essay on a topic. Now write on the same topic, from the other position. Argue against what you just argued.
This makes your critical thinking better, because you force yourself to find arguments, and weakenings, from the other side.
I actually recommend it even more than writing another essay on a new topic. One task, both sides, and only then the next task.
So remember: review, fix, and rewrite. And that's the end of this whole section on how to write an essay. One last workshop, and then the practice tasks.
Now it's your turn. Workshop nineteen, back to your first essay. It's in the card right after this lesson.
Do it before you move on. Each assignment builds on the one before, and by the end of the lessons, you'll have written whole essays.
